abstract.para: Several Btrfs features interact with snapshots and subvolumes. This section describes data deduplication, conversion of other file systems and swap files.

section.title: Data deduplication
section.para: Btrfs supports deduplication by replacing identical blocks with logical links to a single copy of the block. The tool duperemove scans files for identical blocks and submits them for deduplication on a Btrfs file system. Install the package duperemove before you use it.
For large amounts of files, use the option --hashfile. It stores the hashes in a file instead of in RAM.

section.title: Converting other file systems to Btrfs
section.para: The tool btrfs-convert converts an unmounted ext2, ext3, ext4 or ReiserFS file system to Btrfs in place. The tool builds the Btrfs file system in the free space of the original file system and links directly to the existing data. The device needs enough free space for the Btrfs metadata.

The conversion preserves the original file system as a read-only image in a subvolume. The image works like a snapshot and Btrfs does not modify it. To go back to the original file system, run btrfs-convert -r on the device. To remove the image and free its space, delete the subvolume that contains it.

warning.title: Converting the root file system is not supported
warning.para: Converting the root file system to Btrfs is not supported. The process requires a complex configuration for correct rollbacks. Specific subvolumes must exist and /boot must reside on the root file system.
Keep the existing file system or install the system again from scratch.

section.title: Swap files and snapshots
section.para: Btrfs supports swap files if they meet specific requirements. For example, the swap file cannot be compressed, sparse or inline, and the file system must use the single allocation profile. Btrfs cannot create a snapshot of a subvolume that contains an enabled swap file. Place swap files in a subvolume that you do not snapshot.
